Title: Final Walk-Through Checklist — What to Check Before Closing on a House
Description: The final walk-through is your last look before you sign. Bring your contract and inspection report, check that agreed repairs were done and ask for receipts, then run faucets, flush toilets, turn on the heat, flip switches and test outlets and appliances that stay. Look where furniture used to be for new damage. Found a problem? Tell your agent before closing. Read Walter's full final walk-through checklist.

Title: Hanging Christmas Lights? Use Clips, Not Nails or Staples
Description: Nails, tacks and staples driven through or around a light cord can damage the insulation, and you won't see it once the lights are up. Use plastic clips made for holiday lights on gutters, shingles and railings instead. They hold the strings firmly and come off easily in January. Check each string for cracked wires and broken sockets before it goes up. More easy home checks on Walter's page.

Title: Christmas Tree and Holiday Lights Safety — A Simple Checklist
Description: Keep a real tree watered every day and at least 3 feet from fireplaces, heaters, vents and candles. Check light strings for cracked cords and broken sockets before you hang them, use outdoor-rated lights and cords outside, and turn the tree lights off at bedtime and when you leave. A timer makes it automatic. Read Walter's full Christmas tree and holiday lights safety checklist.

Title: Final Walk-Through Tip — Look Where the Furniture Used to Be
Description: By the final walk-through the sellers have usually moved out, so you can finally see the walls and floors that furniture and rugs were covering. Look for scrapes, holes, stains and water marks, and check door frames and stair rails that took a bump on moving day. Take photos of anything new and tell your agent before closing. Title: Ladder Safety for Hanging Christmas Lights
Description: Before you climb to hang lights, look the ladder over for loose rungs, cracks or bent rails. Set it on firm, level ground, lock the spreaders on a stepladder, and have someone hold it. Don't stand on the top steps, keep your belt buckle between the rails, and never set a ladder near overhead power lines. Icy or windy day? Wait. More safety checks on Walter's page.

Title: Replacing an Old Dial Thermostat? It May Contain Mercury
Description: Many older, non-digital thermostats have a small glass bulb of mercury inside. It's sealed and safe on the wall, but don't break it or throw it in the trash when you upgrade. The EPA says to recycle mercury thermostats: check with your local household hazardous waste program or ask your HVAC contractor. If one breaks, follow EPA cleanup guidance. Title: Outdoor Christmas Lights — Use a GFCI Outlet and Outdoor-Rated Cords
Description: Outdoor holiday lights should be labeled for outdoor use, and so should the extension cords. Plug them into a GFCI-protected outlet, and press TEST and RESET first to make sure it works. Keep connections up off snow and puddles, and don't run cords through doors or windows where they get pinched. If a GFCI keeps tripping, unplug things and have an electrician take a look. Title: Seller Made Repairs? Ask for Receipts and Permits Before Closing
Description: If the seller agreed to repairs after your inspection, ask your agent to get the invoices, warranties and any permits before closing, especially for roof, electrical, plumbing, heating or structural work. Then look at the work at the final walk-through and compare it with your inspection report. Not sure it was done right? Ask your inspector or a contractor to take a look. Title: Keep Storage at Least 3 Feet From the Furnace and Water Heater
Description: When the holiday boxes come out of storage, it's easy to stack the empties next to the furnace or water heater. NFPA recommends keeping anything that can burn at least 3 feet from heating equipment. Keep cardboard, paint, paper and cleaning supplies away, and leave a clear path so a technician can reach everything. A five-minute basement tidy. More easy home checks on Walter's page.

Title: 6 Things to Do on Your First Day in a New Home
Description: Just got the keys? On day one, find the main water shutoff and the breaker panel and label them, press the test button on every smoke and CO alarm, and plan to rekey or change the locks. Put in a fresh furnace filter and write the date on it, and look at the label on the water heater so you know its age. Small jobs that make your new house safer. Title: Older Home Basement Stairs — Add a Handrail and Good Light
Description: Basement stairs in older homes are often steep, narrow, without a handrail and lit by a single pull-chain bulb at the bottom. In winter you're up and down them more to check the furnace and laundry. A sturdy handrail and a light switch at the top make a big difference. Loose treads or a wobbly rail? Ask a carpenter to take a look. More older home checks on Walter's free house-age tool.

Title: Don't Burn Wrapping Paper in the Fireplace — Here's Why
Description: It's tempting to toss the wrapping paper into the fire on Christmas morning. Don't. Paper can flare up quickly and send burning pieces up the chimney, and some glossy paper and ribbons don't burn cleanly. Bag it for the trash or recycling instead. Keep stockings, garlands and gift piles well away from the fireplace, and use a screen. More holiday safety checks on Walter's page.

Title: Closing Day — Get Every Key, Code and Remote From the Seller
Description: At closing, make sure you get every key and the things that work like keys: garage door remotes, mailbox and shed keys, alarm codes, and access to any smart locks, doorbells or thermostats. Ask the sellers to remove their accounts from smart devices. Many new owners also have the locks rekeyed after moving in, since you can't know who else has a copy. More buyer tips on Walter's page.

Title: Sewer Smell From a Basement Floor Drain? Pour Water In It
Description: Floor drains in basements and laundry rooms have a trap that holds water to block sewer gas. If the drain is rarely used, that water can dry up, especially with the heat running, and you get a sewer smell. Pour a bucket of water into the drain now and then. If the smell keeps coming back or the drain backs up, call a plumber. More easy home checks on Walter's page.

Title: December Home Maintenance Checklist — 6 Easy Checks
Description: A short December home maintenance checklist: test your smoke and CO alarms, check the furnace filter, water the Christmas tree every day, look under sinks on outside walls for drips, clear snow away from furnace, water heater and dryer vents outside, and peek into the attic with a flashlight for frost on the nails and roof boards. Simple checks for a cozy winter. More monthly checklists on Walter's page.

Title: Older Home With a Wall Furnace? Have It Checked Every Year
Description: Some older homes are heated by a gas wall furnace or floor furnace instead of central heat. Fire safety groups recommend having heating equipment inspected every year by a qualified professional. Keep furniture, curtains and anything that can burn well away from it, never store things against it, and make sure there's a working CO alarm nearby. Title: Heat Pump in Winter — Keep the Outdoor Unit Clear of Snow and Ice
Description: A heat pump's outdoor unit needs air flowing through it to heat your house. After a snowfall, gently brush snow away from the top and sides and keep a clear space around it. Don't chip at ice on the coils or fins, since that can damage them. It's normal to see it defrost now and then, but if it stays covered in ice, call an HVAC technician. Title: Buying a House With Propane Heat? Ask Who Owns the Tank
Description: Many homes with propane heat have a tank that is leased from the gas supplier, not owned by the seller. Before you buy, ask who owns the tank, which company fills it, whether there's a contract, how full it will be at closing, and when it was last inspected. Your agent can add the answers to your paperwork. More buyer tips on Walter's page.

Title: Check That Your Deadbolt Locks All the Way
Description: Lock each outside door and watch the deadbolt. It should slide all the way into the frame smoothly, without pushing, pulling or lifting the door. If it sticks or only goes partway, the door or strike plate may be out of line, often as the house shifts with the seasons. A handy homeowner can adjust the strike plate; otherwise call a locksmith. Title: 5 Questions to Ask About the Heating Before You Buy a House
Description: Buying a house in winter is a good time to ask about the heat. Ask how old the furnace or boiler is and when it was last serviced, what fuel it uses, whether any rooms stay cold, and when the chimney or flue was last checked. Ask for service records, and ask your home inspector or an HVAC pro to look at the system. More buyer tips on Walter's page.

Title: Few Outlets in an Older Home? Don't Plug Power Strips Into Each Other
Description: Many older homes have only one or two outlets per room, and the holidays add lights, trees and chargers. Don't plug power strips or extension cords into each other, and don't run cords under rugs. If plugs feel warm, breakers trip or you see scorch marks, unplug things and call an electrician. Need more outlets? An electrician can add them safely. More older home checks on Walter's free house-age tool.
